title: Why did the machines come to Lancashire and not Bengal?
teaches: Why Britain mechanised cotton first: Allen's high wages and cheap coal, Humphries and Schneider on spinners' earnings, Pomeranz on coal and colonies, Parthasarathi on Indian competition and the British state, Mokyr on useful knowledge

blocks.text: Picture two women spinning cotton in 1770. One lives in a village near Blackburn in Lancashire and spins weft for a local merchant. The other lives in a village in Bengal and spins fine yarn for weavers who supply the East India Company. The Bengali spinner is much the more skilled of the two: her yarn is finer and more even, and Bengal's cloth sells all over the world. A few years earlier, a weaver near Blackburn had built the spinning jenny. Within fifty years, Lancashire's machines would be spinning yarn as fine as Bengal's, and Bengal would be importing British cloth.

Why did the machines appear in Lancashire, a region with a younger and smaller cotton industry, and not in Bengal, Gujarat, the Yangzi delta or France? This is one of the biggest questions in economic history, and historians disagree about the answer. In this lesson we set out five arguments side by side, with their evidence. They are not all exclusive, and most historians combine several.

The economic historian **Robert Allen** argues that the machines were invented where they paid. A machine replaces labour with capital and, later, with energy. It is worth building only where labour is expensive compared with machines and fuel. Allen compiled wages and prices across Europe and Asia and found that in 18th-century Britain wages were high, measured in silver or in what they could buy, while capital was cheap and coal, from the many mines near the surface, was among the cheapest in the world. In such an economy, a machine that saved labour, even at the cost of more capital and coal, returned a profit. In France, and even more in India and China, wages were lower and the same machine returned little or nothing.

Allen's argument also explains why the inventions came in a series. On his figures, early jennies paid well in Britain but barely in France; it took years of further work to make them pay elsewhere, and by then British engineers had improved them further. Most inventions of the period came from practical people who made small improvements over years, and that kind of work happens where the payoff is.

blocks.caption: Whether a spinning jenny paid, with round, illustrative numbers. This tests the first two arguments, which turn on wages; the presets move the wage and price in the direction each suggests and are not the historians' own figures.

blocks.text: **Jane Humphries and Benjamin Schneider** (2019) went back to the earnings of the hand spinners themselves. From more than 2,500 records of spinners' pay and output, they found that women spinners in 18th-century England earned far less than Allen had assumed, often only a few pence a day, and that their earnings did not rise before the jenny and the water frame arrived. If spinners' time was cheap, saving it was worth less, and high wages cannot be the whole explanation. They suggest other motives: making slow spinners more productive and their yarn more even, and easing shortages of yarn that was hard to spin by hand, such as cotton. Allen replied that their records show what spinners earned, not how many hours they worked. Most spinners worked part-time, around other tasks, so low earnings for a day do not mean a low wage for an hour, and he holds that his conclusion stands. The debate continues.

**Kenneth Pomeranz**, in *The Great Divergence* (2000), compared England with the Yangzi delta in China, which in the 18th century was as rich and as commercial as England. He argued that both faced the same limit: land. Food, fuel, fibre and building materials all came from land, which was running short. England escaped the limit through two accidents of geography: coal near the surface, which replaced wood as fuel, and the Americas, whose plantations supplied cotton, sugar and timber. He called the American land Britain drew on **ghost acres**, the land Britain would have needed to produce those goods itself. Raw cotton, lesson 17 shows, came increasingly from plantations worked by enslaved people.

**Prasannan Parthasarathi**, in *Why Europe Grew Rich and Asia Did Not* (2011), looked from India. He argued that Britain mechanised because it faced competition from Indian cloth, which it could not match by hand. Indian producers, with their skills and lower costs, had no such pressure. And the British state did not leave this to the market: the Calico Acts of lesson 12 protected British producers at home, the navy and the East India Company opened markets abroad, and later tariffs kept Indian cloth out while British cloth went into India. Mechanisation was a response to Indian strength, protected by state power.

**Joel Mokyr** emphasises ideas. In the 18th century, Britain had a culture of what he calls useful knowledge: scientific societies, popular lectures, cheap books and journals, and many skilled mechanics and instrument makers who could turn an idea into a working machine. Prices may have told inventors what was worth doing, but they needed the skills and the habits of experiment to do it. In this view the Industrial Revolution was, at bottom, a change in how knowledge was made and shared.

These arguments are not entirely in conflict. Allen and Pomeranz both stress coal; Parthasarathi and Pomeranz both stress Britain's position in a world economy; Humphries and Schneider question one of Allen's numbers rather than every part of his argument; and Mokyr asks why Britain had the people to respond. What historians argue about is the weight of each cause, and whether Britain's lead was a product of its own society or of its place in the world.

Within half a century the trade reversed. British machine-spun yarn became cheaper than Indian hand-spun, then British cloth undercut Indian cloth, first in Europe and Africa and then in India itself, where British goods paid low duties under Company rule. Indian cotton exports fell sharply in the early 19th century, and many spinners and weavers lost their livelihood. How far this deindustrialised India is itself a debate, which lesson 21 takes up.

blocks.caption: Five questions on why Britain mechanised first.

items.ask: In Allen's argument, why would the same jenny pay in Lancashire but not in Bengal?
choices: Labour cost far more next to machines in Lancashire
Bengal's spinners could not learn to work it
Jennies worked only with American cotton
Bengal had no wood or iron to build them
items.why: A machine pays where the labour it saves is expensive compared with what the machine costs. Wages relative to capital were higher in Britain.

items.ask: Humphries and Schneider find that English spinners earned only a few pence a day. Why does that matter for Allen's argument?
choices: Cheap spinners' time makes saving it worth less
It proves the jenny was hardly ever used
It shows most spinners were in fact men
It means coal was dearer than Allen thought
items.why: Allen's case rests on labour being dear. Lower spinners' earnings shrink the jenny's return and leave more to be explained by other causes.

items.ask: What does Pomeranz mean by ghost acres?
choices: Land abroad that grew what Britain's own fields could not
Farms in England abandoned as people moved to the towns
Land in the American South worn out by growing cotton
Common land in England enclosed by landlords for sheep
items.why: American plantations grew the cotton, sugar and timber that would have needed millions of acres in Britain. With coal in place of forests for fuel, they freed Britain from the land limit the Yangzi delta faced.

items.ask: Parthasarathi argues that Britain mechanised because of India. In what sense?
choices: Britain could not match Indian cloth by hand, and the state protected it
Indian engineers designed the first British spinning machines
India banned cotton exports, so Britain had to make its own
Britain copied spinning machines already in use in India
items.why: Competition from superior Indian cloth gave Britain the incentive, and tariffs, bans and empire gave its producers time and markets.

items.ask: Which question does Mokyr's argument answer that the price-based arguments do not?
choices: Why Britain had the skilled people to build the machines
Why wages in Britain were higher than elsewhere
Why coal in Britain was so cheap to mine
Why cotton grew well in the American South
items.why: Prices may show what is worth inventing; Mokyr asks why there were people able to invent it, and points to a culture of useful knowledge.

summary: **Lancashire mechanised first, Bengal did not.** Bengal had the finer industry, but the machines appeared in Britain.
**Allen: machines went where they paid.** High wages, cheap capital and cheap coal made labour-saving machines profitable in Britain.
**Humphries and Schneider: spinners were cheap.** English hand spinners earned less than Allen assumed, so high wages explain less.
**Pomeranz: coal and colonies.** Coal, and the ghost acres of American land, freed Britain from the land limit the Yangzi delta faced.
**Parthasarathi: India pushed and the state protected.** Competition from Indian cloth gave the incentive; bans, tariffs and empire gave British producers room.
**Mokyr: useful knowledge.** A culture of experiment and skilled mechanics turned incentives into machines.
**The arguments overlap.** Historians argue over the weight of each cause, not whether only one is true.
**The trade reversed.** Within fifty years British cloth undercut Indian cloth in India itself.
